claims.text: The sluggish-diffusion paradigm fails in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu are the low-melting-point elements responsible for the proposed surface segregation.
Au and Cu have sufficiently low surface energies to preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-energy gradients create a chemical-potential difference that drives Au and Cu to the surface.
Surface segregation lowers the Gibbs free energy more effectively than configurational entropy stabilizes the bulk FCC lattice.
High surface energy lowers the diffusion activation barrier in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Rapid surface segregation produces a liquid-like surface layer.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate, causing nanoparticle shrinkage.
The nanoparticles become spherical to minimize surface area during heating.
The initial FCC structure of the PLD-grown AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is metastable and kinetically stabilized rather than entropy-stabilized.
Icosahedral nanoparticles have higher initial surface energy than truncated-octahedral nanoparticles.
The critical temperature is controlled by initial nanoparticle surface curvature.
Above a distinct critical temperature, the rate of particle-size reduction accelerates nonlinearly.
Icosahedral particles have a lower critical temperature and faster coalescence or segregation than truncated octahedra.
Departure from the equiatomic composition causes loss of the FCC structure in the particle core.
The composition change caused by selective segregation and evaporation leads to phase separation or amorphization.
Surface-energy terms dominate Gibbs free energy for nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
Bulk entropy terms dominate for nanoparticles larger than 50 nm and for bulk alloys.
High configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion generally prevent segregation and coalescence while preserving FCC structure and particle size.
The starting material consists of sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles made by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane, with elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
